data structures.q: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?
data structures.answer: An array stores elements in contiguous memory, so accessing by index is O(1) and it's cache-friendly, but inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because elements shift, and resizing may copy everything. A linked list stores nodes connected by pointers, so inserting or deleting at a known position is O(1), but access by index is O(n), and the pointers use extra memory.

points.point: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory with constant-time index access.
Linked lists store nodes connected by pointers.
Insertion and deletion are cheaper in linked lists than in the middle of arrays.
Accessing an element by index in a linked list takes linear time.

data structures.q: How does a hash table work, and how are collisions handled?
data structures.answer: A hash table uses a hash function to turn a key into an index in an array of buckets, giving O(1) average-time insert, lookup and delete. Collisions, when two keys map to the same bucket, are handled by chaining, where each bucket holds a list of entries, or open addressing, where you probe for another free slot. When the load factor gets too high the table is resized and entries rehashed. Worst case is O(n) if many keys collide.

points.point: A hash function maps keys to array indexes.
Hash table operations take constant time on average.
Collisions are handled with chaining or open addressing.
The table is resized when the load factor gets too high.

data structures.q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Give real uses of each.
data structures.answer: A stack is last-in, first-out: you push and pop from the same end. It's used for function call stacks, undo, backtracking, depth-first search and matching parentheses. A queue is first-in, first-out: you add at the back and remove from the front. It's used for task scheduling, buffering, breadth-first search and message queues.

points.point: A stack is last-in, first-out.
A queue is first-in, first-out.
Stacks are used for function calls, undo and depth-first search.
Queues are used for scheduling and breadth-first search.

data structures.q: What is a binary search tree, and why does balancing matter?
data structures.answer: In a binary search tree every node's left subtree holds smaller keys and its right subtree larger keys, so search, insert and delete take O(log n) when the tree is balanced, and an in-order traversal returns sorted keys. If keys arrive in sorted order the tree degenerates into a linked list with O(n) operations. Self-balancing trees like AVL and red-black trees rotate nodes to keep the height logarithmic.

points.point: Left children are smaller and right children are larger than the node.
Operations take logarithmic time in a balanced tree.
An unbalanced tree can degrade to linear time like a linked list.
AVL and red-black trees balance themselves with rotations.

data structures.q: What is a heap and where is it used?
data structures.answer: A binary heap is a complete binary tree where each parent is smaller than its children (min-heap) or larger (max-heap), so the minimum or maximum is always at the root. It's stored in an array; insert and remove-top are O(log n) and peeking is O(1). Heaps implement priority queues and are used in Dijkstra's algorithm, scheduling, heap sort, and finding the top k elements.

points.point: In a min-heap each parent is smaller than its children so the minimum is at the root.
Insertion and removal take logarithmic time.
Heaps implement priority queues.
Heaps are used in Dijkstra's algorithm and to find the top k elements.

data structures.q: How are graphs represented, and when would you use each representation?
data structures.answer: An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours; it uses O(V + E) space and suits sparse graphs, which most real graphs are. An adjacency matrix is a V × V grid where cell (i, j) marks an edge; it uses O(V²) space but checks whether an edge exists in O(1), so it suits dense graphs. An edge list is handy for algorithms like Kruskal's.

points.point: An adjacency list stores the neighbours of each vertex.
An adjacency matrix uses a V by V grid.
Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs while matrices suit dense graphs.
A matrix checks for an edge in constant time but uses V squared space.

data structures.q: What is a trie and what problems does it solve?
data structures.answer: A trie, or prefix tree, stores strings character by character, with each path from the root spelling a prefix and nodes marking where words end. Looking up or inserting a word takes O(L) for word length L, independent of how many words are stored, and finding all words with a given prefix is efficient. Tries power autocomplete, spell checking, IP routing with longest-prefix match and word games, at the cost of memory.

points.point: A trie stores strings character by character along paths from the root.
Lookup time depends on the length of the word.
Tries efficiently find all words with a given prefix.
Tries are used for autocomplete and spell checking.

data structures.q: Explain the LRU cache and how you would implement it with O(1) operations.
data structures.answer: An LRU cache has fixed capacity and evicts the least recently used item when full. To get O(1) get and put, combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. On access, move the node to the front; on insert, add at the front and, if over capacity, remove the node at the tail and delete its key from the map.

points.point: An LRU cache evicts the least recently used item when it is full.
A hash map gives constant-time lookup of nodes.
A doubly linked list keeps items ordered by recency.
Accessed items are moved to the front and the tail item is evicted.

data structures.q: What is Big O notation? What are the time complexities of common operations?
data structures.answer: Big O describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows with input size in the worst case, ignoring constants. Common classes are O(1) constant, like array indexing or hash lookups; O(log n), like binary search; O(n), like scanning a list; O(n log n), like efficient sorting; and O(n²), like nested loops comparing all pairs.

points.point: Big O describes how running time grows with input size.
Big O usually describes the worst case and ignores constants.
Binary search is O(log n).
Efficient sorting is O(n log n) and nested loops are O(n squared).

data structures.q: Tell me about a time choosing the right data structure made a big difference in your code.
data structures.answer: A strong answer describes the original approach and why it was slow or awkward, the data structure you switched to (hash set, heap, trie, queue) and why, the complexity improvement, and the measured result.

data structures.q: Describe the hardest data structures or coding problem you've solved, for example in a contest or interview practice.
data structures.answer: A strong answer explains the problem, your first approach and why it fell short, how you reached the better solution, its complexity, and what general technique you took away from it.

data structures.q: Tell me about a time you had to explain a technical concept to someone without a technical background.
data structures.answer: A strong answer sets the context and audience, explains how you simplified the concept (analogies, visuals, focusing on impact), checks understanding, and describes the outcome of the conversation.

algorithms.q: How does binary search work and what is its time complexity?
algorithms.answer: Binary search works on sorted data. It compares the target with the middle element; if they're equal it's found, if the target is smaller it continues in the left half, otherwise the right half. Halving the range each step gives O(log n) time. Watch for off-by-one errors and overflow when computing the midpoint, and it generalises to searching for the first value satisfying a condition.

points.point: Binary search requires sorted data.
Binary search compares with the middle element and discards half the range each step.
Binary search runs in logarithmic time.

algorithms.answer: Both are divide-and-conquer sorts. Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half and merges them; it's always O(n log n), stable, but needs O(n) extra space. Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions elements around it and recurses; it's O(n log n) on average, in-place and usually faster in practice, but O(n²) in the worst case with bad pivots, which random pivots make unlikely. It isn't stable.

points.point: Merge sort is always O(n log n) and stable.
Merge sort needs extra memory.
Quicksort partitions around a pivot and is O(n log n) on average.
Quicksort has a worst case of O(n squared).

algorithms.q: What is the difference between BFS and DFS, and when would you use each?
algorithms.answer: Breadth-first search explores level by level using a queue, so in an unweighted graph it finds the shortest path. Depth-first search follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking, using recursion or a stack; it uses less memory on wide graphs and suits cycle detection, topological sort, connected components and exploring all paths. Both run in O(V + E).

points.point: BFS explores level by level using a queue.
DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking, using a stack or recursion.
BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
DFS is used for cycle detection and topological sort.

algorithms.q: What is dynamic programming? Explain with an example.
algorithms.answer: Dynamic programming solves problems that have overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by solving each subproblem once and storing the result. Memoisation does it top-down with recursion and a cache; tabulation fills a table bottom-up. For example, naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential because it recomputes the same values, while DP computes it in O(n). Knapsack, longest common subsequence and coin change are classic DP problems.

points.point: Dynamic programming applies to problems with overlapping subproblems.
Results of subproblems are stored to avoid recomputation.
Memoisation is top-down while tabulation is bottom-up.
Fibonacci, knapsack and longest common subsequence are classic examples.

algorithms.q: What is a greedy algorithm, and when does it fail?
algorithms.answer: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step without reconsidering, hoping it leads to a global optimum. It works when the problem has the greedy-choice property, as in activity selection, Huffman coding, Dijkstra's algorithm and minimum spanning trees. It fails when local choices can block better global solutions, such as coin change with unusual denominations or the 0/1 knapsack, where dynamic programming is needed.

points.point: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step.
Greedy works for problems like activity selection, Huffman coding or minimum spanning trees.
Greedy can fail to find the global optimum, for example in 0/1 knapsack or some coin change problems.

algorithms.q: How does Dijkstra's algorithm work, and what are its limitations?
algorithms.answer: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source in a weighted graph. It sets all distances to infinity except the source, then repeatedly takes the unvisited node with the smallest known distance from a priority queue and relaxes its edges, updating neighbours' distances if a shorter path is found. With a binary heap it runs in O((V + E) log V). It doesn't work with negative edge weights; Bellman-Ford handles those.

points.point: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source in a weighted graph.
It repeatedly picks the unvisited node with the smallest distance using a priority queue.
It relaxes edges by updating shorter distances to neighbours.
Dijkstra does not work with negative edge weights.

algorithms.q: Explain the two-pointer and sliding window techniques.
algorithms.answer: Two pointers move through data, often from both ends of a sorted array or at different speeds, to avoid nested loops, for example finding a pair with a target sum in O(n) or detecting a cycle with fast and slow pointers. A sliding window keeps a range [left, right] over an array or string, expanding the right side and shrinking the left to maintain a condition, as in the longest substring without repeating characters. Both turn O(n²) brute force into O(n).

points.point: Two pointers move through the data to avoid nested loops.
A sliding window expands and shrinks a range over the data.
These techniques reduce quadratic time to linear time.
Fast and slow pointers detect cycles in a linked list.

algorithms.q: What is recursion, and what are its risks?
algorithms.answer: Recursion is when a function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem until it reaches a base case that returns directly. It fits naturally with trees, divide and conquer and backtracking. Risks are a missing or wrong base case causing infinite recursion, stack overflow from deep recursion because each call uses stack space, and repeated work, which memoisation or an iterative version can fix.

points.point: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem.
Recursion needs a base case to stop.
Deep recursion can cause a stack overflow.

algorithms.q: How would you detect a cycle in a directed graph, and how does topological sort relate to it?
algorithms.answer: Run DFS while tracking each node's state: unvisited, in the current recursion stack, or finished. Reaching a node that's still in the current stack means a back edge, so there's a cycle. Topological sort orders nodes so every edge points forward, and exists only for directed acyclic graphs. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree zero; if some nodes are never removed, the graph has a cycle. It's used for dependency resolution like build systems and course scheduling.

points.point: DFS detects a cycle when it reaches a node already in the current recursion stack.
Topological sort only exists for directed acyclic graphs.
Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree zero.
Topological sort is used for dependency resolution and scheduling.

algorithms.q: Tell me about a time you improved an algorithm's efficiency in real code.
algorithms.answer: A strong answer explains the slow code and its complexity, how you identified the bottleneck, the better algorithm or data structure, the new complexity, and the measured speed-up on real data.

algorithms.q: Walk me through how you approach a coding problem you haven't seen before.
algorithms.answer: A strong answer covers clarifying requirements and edge cases, working through examples, starting with a brute-force solution, looking for patterns to optimise, analysing complexity, writing clean code, and testing it with edge cases — ideally illustrated with a real example.

algorithms.q: Describe a time your solution had a subtle bug that only appeared on edge cases.
algorithms.answer: A strong answer describes the bug and the edge case that triggered it (empty input, overflow, duplicates, off-by-one), how you found it, the fix, and how you now test for such cases.

system design.q: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.
system design.answer: Clarify requirements: create short links, redirect quickly, maybe custom aliases and analytics; reads far outnumber writes. Generate a short key by base62-encoding a unique ID from a counter or ID generator, or hashing with collision checks. Store key-to-URL mappings in a key-value or NoSQL store that scales horizontally. Put a cache like Redis in front for hot links, and return HTTP 301 or 302 redirects. Add rate limiting and record clicks asynchronously for analytics.

points.point: Short keys are generated with base62 encoding of a unique ID or a hash.
The system is read-heavy, so a cache is used for popular links.
Mappings are stored in a scalable key-value or NoSQL database.
The service redirects with HTTP 301 or 302.

system design.q: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
system design.answer: Vertical scaling adds more CPU, memory or disk to a single machine; it's simple but hits hardware limits, gets expensive and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads load across them with a load balancer; it scales further and improves availability, but the application must be stateless or handle distributed state.

points.point: Vertical scaling adds more resources to a single machine.
Horizontal scaling adds more machines.
Vertical scaling has hardware limits and a single point of failure.
Horizontal scaling needs a load balancer and stateless services.

system design.answer: The CAP theorem says a distributed system can't guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance all at once. Since network partitions will happen, the real choice during a partition is between consistency, where every read sees the latest write or gets an error, and availability, where every request gets a response that may be stale. Banking systems often prefer CP, while social feeds or shopping carts often prefer AP with eventual consistency.

points.point: CAP stands for consistency, availability and partition tolerance.
A distributed system cannot guarantee all three at the same time.
During a network partition you must choose between consistency and availability.
AP systems often use eventual consistency.

system design.q: Where and how would you use caching in a system?
system design.answer: Caches sit at many layers: browser and CDN caches for static assets, an application-level cache like Redis or Memcached for frequent database reads or expensive computations, and the database's own buffer cache. Common patterns are cache-aside and write-through. You need an invalidation strategy with TTLs or explicit eviction to avoid stale data, an eviction policy like LRU, and protection against cache stampedes.

points.point: A CDN caches static content close to users.
An in-memory cache like Redis reduces database load.
Cache invalidation with TTLs prevents stale data.
Eviction policies like LRU decide what to remove.

system design.q: How do load balancers work, and what algorithms do they use?
system design.answer: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple servers to spread load and improve availability, using health checks to stop sending traffic to unhealthy servers. Algorithms include round robin, weighted round robin, least connections and IP hash for stickiness. Layer 4 balancers route by IP and port, while layer 7 balancers understand HTTP and can route by path or header and terminate TLS.

points.point: A load balancer distributes traffic across multiple servers.
Health checks remove unhealthy servers from rotation.
Algorithms include round robin and least connections.
Layer 7 load balancers can route based on HTTP content.

system design.q: How would you design a rate limiter?
system design.answer: Decide what to limit, such as per user, API key or IP, and where, usually at an API gateway or middleware. Algorithms include the token bucket, which allows bursts up to a capacity while refilling at a steady rate, leaky bucket, fixed window counters (simple but bursty at window edges) and sliding window logs or counters. In a distributed system store counters in a shared fast store like Redis with atomic operations, return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, and decide whether to fail open or closed if the store is down.

points.point: The token bucket algorithm allows bursts while refilling at a fixed rate.
Fixed and sliding window counters are alternative algorithms.
Counters are stored in a shared store like Redis for distributed systems.
Rejected requests receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

system design.q: What is database sharding and what problems does it introduce?
system design.answer: Sharding splits data horizontally across multiple databases by a shard key, so each holds a subset of rows and the system can scale writes and storage beyond one machine. Strategies include range-based, hash-based and directory-based sharding; consistent hashing reduces data movement when adding shards. Problems include hot shards from a skewed key, expensive cross-shard queries and joins, distributed transactions, and difficult resharding.

points.point: Sharding splits data across multiple databases using a shard key.
Data can be sharded by range or by hash.
A poor shard key can create hot spots.
Cross-shard queries, joins and transactions become difficult.

system design.q: Design a notification system that sends email, SMS and push notifications.
system design.answer: Services call a notification API that validates the request, checks user preferences and opt-outs, renders templates, and puts messages on a message queue, with separate queues or topics per channel. Workers consume them and call providers like an email service, an SMS gateway, or APNs and FCM for push. Use retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue for failures, idempotency keys to avoid duplicates, rate limiting per user, and track delivery status and analytics.

points.point: A message queue decouples producers from the sending workers.
Workers send through third-party providers for each channel.
Failed sends are retried, with a dead-letter queue for permanent failures.
User preferences and opt-outs are respected.
Idempotency prevents duplicate notifications.

system design.q: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases, and how do you choose?
system design.answer: SQL databases store structured data in tables with a fixed schema, support joins and ACID transactions, and suit data with clear relationships, like orders and payments. NoSQL databases (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) have flexible schemas and scale horizontally more easily, often trading strict consistency for availability and speed. Choose based on data shape, query patterns, consistency needs and scale; many systems use both.

points.point: SQL databases use structured tables with a fixed schema.
SQL databases support joins and ACID transactions.
NoSQL databases have flexible schemas and scale horizontally.
The choice depends on data shape, query patterns and consistency needs.

system design.q: Tell me about the architecture of a system you built. What would you change today?
system design.answer: A strong answer walks through the components and data flow, explains the key design decisions and trade-offs, describes how it handled scale and failures, and honestly names what you'd do differently with hindsight and why.

system design.q: Describe a time a system you worked on had to handle much more load than expected.
system design.answer: A strong answer covers what caused the spike, what broke first, how you diagnosed it under pressure, the short-term mitigation (scaling, caching, rate limiting, degrading features), the long-term fix, and lessons learned.

system design.q: Tell me about a technical decision where you had to weigh trade-offs and convince others.
system design.answer: A strong answer explains the decision and the options, the criteria you used (cost, complexity, performance, team skills), how you gathered evidence (prototype, benchmark), how you persuaded people or handled disagreement, and how the decision turned out.

testing.q: What is the difference between unit, integration and end-to-end tests?
testing.answer: Unit tests check a single function or class in isolation, with dependencies mocked; they're fast and pinpoint failures. Integration tests check that several components work together, such as code with a real database. End-to-end tests run the whole application like a user would, through the UI or API; they give the most confidence but are slow and brittle. The test pyramid suggests many unit tests, fewer integration tests and a few end-to-end tests.

points.point: Unit tests test individual functions or classes in isolation.
Integration tests check that components work together.
End-to-end tests test the whole application like a user.
The test pyramid has many unit tests and few end-to-end tests.

testing.q: What are mocks and stubs, and when should you use them?
testing.answer: Test doubles replace real dependencies in tests. A stub returns canned responses so the code under test can run; a mock also records how it was called so the test can verify interactions. Use them for slow, external or non-deterministic dependencies like network calls, payment providers or the clock. Overusing mocks couples tests to implementation details and can hide integration bugs.

points.point: Mocks and stubs replace real dependencies in tests.
A stub returns predefined responses.
A mock verifies how it was called.
Overusing mocks makes tests brittle and can hide bugs.

testing.answer: In TDD you write a failing test before the code, write the minimum code to make it pass, then refactor while keeping tests green: red, green, refactor. It drives a design that's easy to test, gives fast feedback and leaves a full regression suite behind. It works best when requirements are clear and can feel slow for exploratory work.

points.point: In TDD you write a failing test before writing the code.
TDD follows the red, green, refactor cycle.
TDD leads to better design and a regression test suite.

testing.q: What makes a good unit test?
testing.answer: Good unit tests are fast, isolated and deterministic, so they give the same result every time and don't depend on order or external systems. Each test checks one behaviour, has a descriptive name, and follows arrange, act, assert. They test behaviour through the public interface rather than implementation details, cover edge cases and error paths, and are easy to read.

points.point: Good tests are fast and deterministic.
Good tests are independent and isolated from each other.
Tests follow arrange, act, assert and check one behaviour.
Tests should cover edge cases and error paths.

testing.q: What is code coverage, and is 100% coverage a good goal?
testing.answer: Coverage measures which lines or branches run during tests. It's useful for finding untested code, especially risky logic. But 100% doesn't mean the code is correct: tests can execute lines without asserting anything meaningful, and chasing the number leads to low-value tests. Branch coverage is more informative than line coverage, and mutation testing checks whether tests actually catch bugs.

points.point: Code coverage measures which code is executed by tests.
High coverage does not guarantee correctness.
Branch coverage is more informative than line coverage.
Mutation testing checks whether tests catch bugs.

testing.q: How do you deal with flaky tests?
testing.answer: Treat them as bugs: track and quarantine them so they don't block everyone, then find the root cause. Common causes are timing and race conditions (fixed sleeps instead of proper waits), shared state or order dependence between tests, reliance on external services, real time and dates, and randomness. Fix with explicit waits, isolating state, mocking external dependencies and seeding randomness, and avoid simply adding automatic retries that hide real problems.

points.point: Flaky tests should be tracked, quarantined and fixed rather than ignored.
Timing issues and fixed sleeps cause flakiness.
Shared state or test order dependence causes flakiness.
External services, time and randomness cause flakiness.

testing.q: Tell me about a time tests caught a serious bug before it reached production.
testing.answer: A strong answer describes the change, which test caught it and why it existed, what the impact would have been, and how it reinforced or changed your testing approach.

testing.q: Describe how you improved testing on a project that had little or no test coverage.
testing.answer: A strong answer covers the starting point and risks, how you prioritised what to test (critical paths, frequent bugs), how you introduced tests without stopping delivery, how you got the team on board, and the measurable improvement in bugs or confidence.

selenium.q: What is Selenium WebDriver and how does it work?
selenium.answer: Selenium WebDriver automates real browsers for testing web applications. Test code in Java, Python or another language sends commands through the WebDriver protocol to a browser-specific driver such as ChromeDriver or GeckoDriver, which controls the browser. Selenium Grid runs tests in parallel across machines and browsers.

points.point: Selenium WebDriver automates web browsers for testing.
Browser-specific drivers like ChromeDriver control the browser.
Selenium supports multiple programming languages.
Selenium Grid runs tests in parallel across browsers.

selenium.q: What is the difference between implicit and explicit waits?
selenium.answer: An implicit wait sets a global timeout for finding elements, so every lookup polls until the element appears or time runs out. An explicit wait waits for a specific condition on a specific element using WebDriverWait with expected conditions, like element to be clickable. Explicit waits are more precise and reliable; mixing the two can cause unpredictable delays, and Thread.sleep should be avoided.

points.point: An implicit wait applies a global timeout to all element lookups.
An explicit wait waits for a specific condition using WebDriverWait.
Fixed sleeps like Thread.sleep should be avoided.
Mixing implicit and explicit waits can cause unpredictable timing.

selenium.q: What locator strategies does Selenium support, and which are best?
selenium.answer: Selenium can find elements by ID, name, class name, tag name, link text, CSS selector and XPath. Stable unique IDs or dedicated test attributes like data-testid are best, then concise CSS selectors. Long absolute XPaths that depend on page structure are brittle and break with small layout changes.

points.point: Locators include ID, name, class, CSS selector and XPath.
Unique IDs or test attributes are the most reliable locators.
Absolute XPaths are brittle.

selenium.q: What is the Page Object Model?
selenium.answer: The Page Object Model represents each page or component as a class that holds its locators and exposes methods for user actions, like login(username, password). Tests call these methods instead of using locators directly. This removes duplication, makes tests read like user flows, and means a UI change requires updating only one page class.

points.point: Each page is represented by a class containing its locators and actions.
Tests use page methods instead of locators directly.
UI changes only need updates in one place, which improves maintainability.

selenium.q: How do you make a large Selenium test suite reliable and fast?
selenium.answer: Use explicit waits, stable locators and the Page Object Model so tests don't break on timing or layout. Make tests independent with their own data, set up state through APIs instead of the UI, and run them in parallel on Selenium Grid or a cloud service, headless in CI. Keep the end-to-end suite focused on critical user journeys, push other checks down to unit and API tests, and capture screenshots and logs on failure.

points.point: Explicit waits and stable locators reduce flakiness.
Tests run in parallel, for example with Selenium Grid.
Test data and setup are created through APIs rather than the UI.
Headless browsers speed up runs in CI.
Screenshots on failure help debugging.

selenium.q: Tell me about a test automation framework you built or maintained.
selenium.answer: A strong answer explains the application under test, the framework design (language, Page Object Model, reporting, CI integration), how you kept it reliable, the coverage achieved, and its impact on releases.

selenium.q: Describe a time you reduced flakiness in an automated UI test suite.
selenium.answer: A strong answer covers how flaky the suite was and its cost, how you identified the causes (timing, data, environment), the fixes (explicit waits, isolated data, retries only where justified), and the measured improvement in pass rate.
